notes:
I ran out of searches and fetches before reaching Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), wesley.nnu.edu, oca.org and newadvent.org, and I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those are left out below. The Catholic notes come from the Haydock Catholic Commentary on biblehub. Pages I read in full have no citation tags, but each point gives its URL.

## Verse-by-verse notes

**v. 1**
- The angel is the interpreting angel. "Came again and waked me" probably just means "roused me again." The prophet had sunk into a stupor after the last vision, as Daniel did and as the apostles did at the Transfiguration. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) says the prophet lay in an ecstatic slumber, astonished by the previous vision, and "came again" is an idiom for "waked me again," not a sign the angel had left. Keil and Delitzsch disagree: the angel had left after the earlier visions and now came back. Matthew Poole takes the angel to be Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-1.htm

**v. 2**
- The angel makes the prophet describe what he sees, then explains it. This lampstand differs from the tabernacle one in three ways: a central bowl of oil, pipes, and a supply from olive trees. The Hebrew "seven and seven pipes" is debated (49? 14? seven per lamp?). The point either way is a plentiful supply that needs no priest to refill it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- The NET Bible's note pictures "fourteen pipes going to the lamps": two pipes to each of the seven lamps. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Zec&chapter=4
- David Guzik notes that tending the temple lamps was tiresome work: refilling, cleaning soot, trimming wicks. Here Zechariah sees "self-filling" lamps fed straight from two olive trees. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-4/
- Ligonier says the vision meant God would certainly build His house, since the lampstand would be useless without the temple. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/zechariah-sees-new-lampstand

**v. 3**
- The olive trees drip oil from their branches into channels feeding the bowl, something never seen in the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-4/
- Meredith Kline (Reformed) takes a less common view: the trees stand for God's glorious Presence, arching over the lampstand the way the cherubim spread their wings over the ark. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/bymyspirit.html

**v. 4**
- John Gill says Zechariah knew what the objects were; he wanted to know what they meant. Benson notes his respect in calling the angel "lord": those who want to be taught should honour their teachers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-4.htm
- What "these" refers to is debated. Some say the olive trees, others the lamps. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-4-commentary The NET note says it must refer to the lamps, because the trees are explained later. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Zec&chapter=4

**v. 5**
- The angel is not so much surprised at the prophet's slowness as drawing his full attention to what comes next. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- Haydock quotes Menochius: "Thou art a prophet, and art thou ignorant?" https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/zechariah/4.htm

**v. 6**
- This is the heart of the vision. The work will be done by God's grace alone. "Might" is rendered "an army" in the Vulgate. The oil pictures the Spirit's grace: the lamps are fed without human hands, and the work will be too. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- Guzik: "might" is collective strength, "power" is individual strength. Chapter 3 dealt with purity, but God's work also needs resources, and not human ones. The supply should be continual. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-4/
- Adam Clarke: not by might (your own) nor by power (authority from others), but by the providence, power and energy of the Most High. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/nas/zechariah/4-6.html
- The Targum (the ancient Aramaic paraphrase) reads "by my Word" instead of "by my Spirit." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/4.htm

**v. 7**
- The "great mountain" is a figure for all the difficulties in Zerubbabel's way. Pulpit questions whether a temple could have a "topstone." It prefers a cornerstone, or just a picture of finishing the work. The shout means "God's favour rest upon it!" The Targum reads the verse as messianic. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- Guzik suggests the mountain may literally be the pile of rubble at the temple site, and that "Grace, grace" means the credit is all God's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-4/
- Poole names the mountain as Sanballat and his allies, or Satan, or Babylon. The Geneva notes say Zerubbabel represented Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-7.htm
- NET: the mountain is the enormous task of rebuilding the temple and setting up the messianic kingdom. "Grace" fits because the work is done by God's gracious Spirit. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Zec&chapter=4
- Haydock (Challoner) says the mountain is the enemies' opposition, or perhaps Zion lying in ruins. The Vulgate reads "equal grace" (grace added to grace). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/zechariah/4.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- The word came through the interpreting angel and spells out what the vision showed in pictures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- History: the foundation was laid in the second year after the return (Ezra 3:8). Opposition stopped the work until Darius's second year, and it was finished in his sixth year (Ezra 6:15). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-9.htm
- Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship) notes that Zechariah names Zerubbabel only in 4:6–10, where he alone starts and finishes the temple, by divine spirit rather than human power. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/dictionary/zerubbabel/

**v. 10**
- The "small things" are the temple's poor beginnings (Haggai 2:3). Pulpit says the grammar makes the seven eyes the ones who rejoice. The plumb line is literally "the stone, the tin." The eyes stand for God's watchful providence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- NET: the Hebrew word more likely means a "tin tablet", after the ancient custom of putting inscribed tin plates in foundation deposits. The eyes speak of God's knowing all things. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Zec&chapter=4
- Guzik: Zerubbabel still needed the plumb line. God did not take a miraculous shortcut, because His work in Zerubbabel mattered as much as His work through him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-4/
- JFB: God rebukes their ungrateful unbelief over such a humble start. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-10.htm
- Haydock: the eyes are God's providence, or (Calmet) the seven chief angels. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/zechariah/4.htm

**vv. 11–13**
- The angel delays his answer to sharpen the prophet's desire and make him ask more precisely. The "branches" are literally "ears," as of grain, and the oil is called "gold" for its colour. In v. 13 the angel stresses where the community's power comes from. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/zechariah/4.htm
- NET translates "branches" as "extensions," probably meaning the olives themselves. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Zec&chapter=4
- Haydock (Worthington): the branches are Christ's divine and human natures. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/zechariah/4.htm

**v. 14**
- Hebrew "sons of fresh oil" rather than the usual word for "anointed." In context the phrase means Joshua the priest and Zerubbabel the governor. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Zec&chapter=4 Clarke agrees: one serves in church matters, the other in civil. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/4-14.html
- Pulpit: they are the royal and priestly powers, though the text avoids naming people so the picture is not limited to two individuals. It cites Revelation 11:4. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-14.htm
- Cambridge Bible: the angel may deliberately avoid a human meaning; these could be agencies near God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-14.htm
- Matthew Henry: Christ is the Olive Tree, the Spirit the Olive Branch. Gill: possibly Christ and the Holy Spirit. Poole lists other views (Enoch and Elijah, Peter and Paul) and finally determines nothing. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-14.htm

## Where the traditions differ

- **v. 6, the Spirit.** Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) reads it as the church being built not by the power of man's free will, but by the effective grace of the Spirit. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/zechariah/4.htm Calvin: when earthly help fails, rely on God alone. Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) says the church errs in pushing programs. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/4-6.html
- **The lampstand: Israel or the Church?** John MacArthur: Israel, with the church only temporarily in that role. https://www.preceptaustin.org/zechariah-4-commentary Pulpit and Cyril: the Church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/zechariah/4-14.htm
- **The two olive trees and Revelation 11.** Guzik: future witnesses immediately before Jesus' return. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/zechariah-4/ Wordsworth: the Law and the Gospel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/zechariah/4-11.html Ellicott: Zerubbabel and Joshua, or Zechariah and Haggai, but the picture applies in every age. https://biblehub.com/revelation/11-4.htm
- **Christ.** Kline: at Pentecost Jesus, the true son of oil, poured out the Spirit. https://www.monergism.com/thethreshold/articles/onsite/bymyspirit.html

## Other views

- **Modern scholarship.** NET says it is premature to read "Spirit" in v. 6 as the third Person of the Trinity, though the Old Testament prepares the way. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Zec&chapter=4
- **Catholic.** The lampstand is the temple and, in a higher sense, Christ's Church. Most interpreters take the olives as Enoch and Elijah (Revelation 11). Church and state should cooperate, as Joshua and Zerubbabel did. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/haydock/zechariah/4.htm
